x: Option C is incorrect: a merger protects members from disqualification only if at least two-thirds of the legislature party agree. The one-third 'split' exception was removed by the 91st Amendment (2003).
t: Discriminate the two-thirds merger rule from the abolished one-third split.

x: Both are true: the one-third split exception no longer exists because the 91st Amendment (2003) removed it. R explains A.
t: Recall the 91st Amendment's change to the Tenth Schedule.

x: The Congress was founded in 1885, the CPI in 1925, the Jana Sangh in 1951, and the CPI(M) after the 1964 split. The order is B, D, C, A.
t: Recall the years 1885, 1925, 1951 and 1964.

x: W.C. Banerjee was the Congress's first president, Syama Prasad Mookerjee founded the Jana Sangh, Vajpayee was the BJP's first president, and Pawar, Sangma and Anwar formed the NCP. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each party to its founder.

x: I and II are correct: the BJP was formed in 1980 as the Jana Sangh's successor, and the BSP in 1984. III is false because the Samajwadi Party was formed in 1992; 1998 is the Trinamool Congress.
t: Recall the years parties were founded.

x: Political scientist Rajni Kothari coined 'one-party dominant system', or 'Congress system', for the post-independence pattern.
t: Recall Rajni Kothari.

x: Both are true: the 'Congress system' meant one party dominating a competitive, multi-party democracy. R gives that meaning, so R explains A.
t: Recall Kothari's idea of the Congress system.

x: The 1989 general election ended the Congress system and began the era of minority and coalition governments.
t: Recall the 1989 turning point.

x: Both are true: after 1989, V.P. Singh led the National Front government, supported from outside by the BJP and the Left.
t: Recall the National Front's outside support.

x: The Leader of the Opposition was first formally recognised in 1969.
t: Recall the year the post was formally recognised.

x: To be recognised as Leader of the Opposition, the largest opposition party needs at least 10% of the House, about 55 Lok Sabha seats.
t: Recall the 10% rule.

x: Political parties entered the Constitution through the 52nd Amendment (1985), which added the Tenth Schedule on anti-defection. They were not in the original text.
t: Recall the 52nd Amendment and the Tenth Schedule.

x: Under the second route to national-party status, a party needs both 6% of votes in four States and four Lok Sabha seats.
t: Recall the 6% and four-seat route.

x: The Congress was founded in 1885, the BJP in 1980, the BSP in 1984 and the Trinamool Congress in 1998. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the years parties were founded.

x: Five were formed in 1980 or later: BJP (1980), BSP (1984), SP (1992), TMC (1998) and NCP (1999). The CPI dates from 1925.
t: Check each party's year against 1980.

x: Both are true: the merger exception protects members from disqualification, and it applies only when two-thirds of the legislature party agree. R explains A.
t: Recall the two-thirds merger rule.

x: The CPI was formed in 1925, Syama Prasad Mookerjee founded the Jana Sangh, and Vajpayee was the BJP's first president. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii.
t: Match each party to its founder or year.

x: AITC stands for All India Trinamool Congress.
t: Expand the abbreviation.

x: The All India Trinamool Congress is also known as TMC.
t: Recall the party's short name.

x: The anti-defection bill was passed on 15 February 1985 and took effect on 1 March 1985.
t: Discriminate the date passed from the date in force.

x: Both are true: the 52nd Amendment first named political parties in the Constitution, and it added the Tenth Schedule. Adding the Schedule is the change itself, not the reason parties were recognised, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether describing the amendment explains its effect.

x: The 52nd Amendment changed Articles 101 and 102 for Parliament and 190 and 191 for State Legislatures. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Pair the Union Articles (101, 102) with the State ones (190, 191).

x: Option C is incorrect: Jammu and Kashmir passed its own anti-defection law in 1979, before the national law of 1985.
t: Recall J&K's 1979 law.

x: All three are correct: the 91st Amendment (2003) strengthened the anti-defection law, removed the one-third split, and capped the ministry at 15% of the lower House.
t: Recall the 91st Amendment's changes.

x: Both are true: a member can be held to have given up party membership without resigning, because conduct such as campaigning for a rival party counts. R explains A.
t: Recall that conduct can amount to giving up membership.

x: A is false: the President and Governor have no role in Tenth Schedule cases. B is true: the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides them.
t: Recall who decides defection cases.

x: A party member is disqualified for defying the whip, an independent for joining any party, a nominated member for joining a party after six months, and a presiding officer for joining another party. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Match each kind of member to the act that disqualifies them.

x: All three are correct: a member is protected with prior permission, if the party condones the vote within 15 days, or in a merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party.
t: Recall the three safeguards.

x: J&K passed its law in 1979, the bill was passed on 15 February 1985, it took effect on 1 March 1985, and the 91st Amendment came in 2003. The order is A, B, C, D.
t: Recall the dates 1979, 1985 and 2003.

x: Both are true: the ECI is not consulted on defection, because the Speaker or Chairman decides as a tribunal. R explains A.
t: Discriminate defection cases (no ECI) from other disqualifications (ECI opinion).

x: The Tenth Schedule sets no time limit for the presiding officer to decide a defection petition, which is often criticised.
t: Recall that there is no time limit.

x: Defection cases for MPs and State legislators go to the Speaker or Chairman. Other disqualifications go to the President for MPs and the Governor for MLAs and MLCs. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Discriminate defection (Speaker) from other disqualification (President or Governor).

x: A is false: the one-third split exception was abolished in 2003. B is true: a merger is protected when two-thirds of the legislature party agree.
t: Discriminate the two-thirds merger rule from the abolished one-third split.

x: In Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the Supreme Court held that the presiding officer's Tenth Schedule decisions are open to judicial review.
t: Recall Kihoto Hollohan.

x: The anti-defection law took effect on 1 March 1985, after the bill was passed on 15 February 1985.
t: Discriminate the date passed from the date in force.

x: Both are true: an independent member is disqualified if they join any party after election, but they may become a Minister without joining a party. Only taking party membership disqualifies them.
t: Discriminate joining a party from joining the government.

x: An independent member is disqualified only on joining a political party. So becoming a Minister after taking party membership disqualifies them, while becoming one as an independent does not.
t: Remember that only party membership disqualifies an independent.

x: Option A is incorrect: a presiding officer may give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin the party after leaving office. Joining another party, during or after the term, disqualifies them.
t: Discriminate rejoining the original party from joining another.

x: Defection disqualification comes under Article 102(2) for MPs and 191(2) for State legislators, read with the Tenth Schedule. Clauses (1) are the general grounds.
t: Discriminate clause (1) (general) from clause (2) (defection).

x: Article 102(1) gives an MP's general disqualifications, decided by the President under 103. Article 191(1) gives a State legislator's, decided by the Governor under 192. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Pair Articles 102 and 103 (Union) with 191 and 192 (State).

x: All four disqualify: a party member giving up membership, an independent joining a party, a nominated member joining after six months, and a presiding officer joining another party.
t: Match each kind of member to the act that disqualifies them.

x: For both, the ECI's opinion is compulsory and binding: the President decides for MPs and the Governor for MLAs and MLCs. The answer is a-i, b-iii.
t: Recall that the ECI's opinion binds both.

x: A 'party-elected member' means an MP or MLA elected on a party ticket.
t: Recall the categories of member.
